status: complete first edition (2026-10-08). Bibliography verified from catalogs, copyright records and the UW finding aid; topical facts come from public sources that draw on Wood, plus Wood's 1990 Columbia article (read in full). Page-level checking inside Wood's books is the main open task; see 'uncertain'. Verified 2026-10-08 (see VERIFY.md): no sentence of Wood is stored here; three close paraphrases of his 1990 Columbia article and two epitaph seeds were reworded.
compiled_for: Olympic Peninsula Hiker (design-stage). Knowledge-base backbone built on the work of Robert L. Wood.
how_to_use: Every fact here is restated in our own words. Facts are not copyrightable; Wood's sentences are. Nothing in this file is a quotation from Wood.

In the topical index each fact has a 'wood' list naming the Wood work that is the go-to account for it (with page or chapter where a locator exists) so the game can credit him, and a 'corroboration' list of URLs we actually read. Unless a citation's locator_basis is 'read_by_us', we did NOT read the fact in Wood's own text (his books are not openly online); we read it in the corroborating sources, several of which draw on Wood. Check the book before printing a page number in the game.

Locators marked locator_basis='cited_by_evans_1983' come from page citations in Gail H. E. Evans, Historic Resource Study: Olympic National Park (NPS, 1983), a U.S. government work that cites Wood by page. They were not checked against the book itself.
Locators marked locator_basis='google_books_toc' come from the table-of-contents snippet Google Books shows for that edition.
Use 'node_index' at the bottom to go from a map node id to the Wood topics that touch it.
Before shipping any line of text that paraphrases a Wood fact, keep the credit line; before shipping any verbatim Wood text, get written permission (see 'permissions').

copyright_policy.rule: Never copy Robert L. Wood's sentences into game files. Use his books for facts only, restated in our own words, and credit the title.
copyright_policy.why: All of Wood's Olympic books and articles are still in copyright (see each work's 'copyright' block). Pre-1978 titles carried notices and were automatically renewed under the 1992 Copyright Renewal Act, so they run 95 years from publication (first edition of Across the Olympic Mountains: through 2062). Post-1978 titles run at least to the end of 2073 (Wood died in 2003; life + 70).
verbatim_quotes_allowed_only_from: U.S. government works (e.g., Lt. Joseph P. O'Neil's report printed as Senate Doc. 59, 54th Congress, 1st Session, 1896; Evans's 1983 NPS Historic Resource Study).
Texts published in the U.S. before 1931 (e.g., the Seattle Press of July 16, 1890; The Mountaineer annuals of 1907).
Wood's own text only with written permission from the current rights holders (see 'permissions').
copyright_policy.note_on_quotes_inside_wood: Wood's books quote explorers' diaries and newspapers. Those inner quotes may be public domain at their source, but copy them only from the original source text (with URL), never from Wood's page, because Wood's transcription, selection and editing are his. Some diaries (e.g., Harry Fisher's 1890 journal) survive only as manuscripts whose literary rights were not transferred to the University of Washington; treat them as needing permission until checked.

epitaph_feature.user_request: After a death: write our own epitaph or tap a random Robert Wood sentence.
epitaph_feature.decision_for_now: Ship ORIGINAL epitaphs only. A 'random Robert Wood sentence' cannot ship unless the rights holders grant written permission; until then the Wood option should draw from 'epitaph_fact_seeds' below (a fact Wood documented, retold in our words, with a credit line such as 'After Robert L. Wood, Across the Olympic Mountains (1967)').
epitaph_feature.if_permission_is_obtained: Store each licensed Wood sentence in a separate file (e.g., lore/wood_licensed_lines.json) with title, edition, page, the permission letter's date and scope (media, territory, term, credit wording). Do not mix licensed text into this file.
epitaph_feature.public_domain_alternative: Short lines from the explorers themselves (Seattle Press 1890 report, O'Neil's 1896 Senate report, The Mountaineer 1907) may be used verbatim once copied from a fetched primary text with URL; that collection belongs in a separate quotes file, not here.

summary_own_words: Seattle-area writer who spent about half a century walking, climbing and researching the Olympic Mountains, and who became their main historian of exploration and the author of the standard backcountry trail guide.

He first saw the Olympics in 1946 (publisher bio). The UW finding aid says he moved to Seattle in 1946; the Seattle Times death notice (seen only via a search summary) says he moved to Seattle in 1961. Both can be true if he lived elsewhere in the region (he studied at Olympic College in Bremerton in the 1950s) before settling in Seattle; treat the 1961 date as unconfirmed.

During the war he trained at Fort Knox (1943), studied in the Army Specialized Training Program at the University of Dayton (about Sept. 1943 - June 1944), was then reclassified to limited service for medical reasons and worked at the military prison at Fort Hood, Texas, as secretary to the prison psychiatrist (per his own notes in the UW inventory).

He took classes at the University of Washington (a spring-1948 English term paper on the Olympic rain forest was, in his words in the inventory, the seed of his later books) and later creative-writing and mountaineering classes at Olympic College in Bremerton (1956-57).

He earned his living as a shorthand (Stenotype) reporter; the Seattle Times death notice (via search summary) says he worked as a stenographer for the King County courts until retiring in 1980. His papers hold a Superior Court notice to court staff about his books. He wrote for the trade magazines The National Shorthand Reporter and The Blank Space.
He climbed Mount Olympus many times (the death notice, via search summary, says eighteen ascents).

In August 1961 a 'Bob Wood' with Doug Waali and Kent Heathershaw made what were reported as first ascents in the Bailey Range: Mount Childs (Aug. 6), Mount Pulitzer, and Stephen Peak (Aug. 8). Waali also appears in Wood's papers, so this is very probably the same man (AAJ 1962).
He gave his papers to the University of Washington Libraries in 1972, 1985 and 2000; literary rights in those PAPERS were transferred to UW.

After his death the copyrights in his published works passed, by inheritance and written agreement, to Tom and Jessica Tonne of Snohomish (Copyright Office record for the 2020 trail guide; Sequim Gazette 2016), who appointed Bill Hoke to edit the fourth edition of the trail guide.

books.what_it_covers_own_words: The full story of the Seattle Press's 1889-90 winter crossing of the Olympics: why the newspaper sent the party (Governor-elect Elisha P. Ferry's call to explore the range), who the six men were, their months in the Elwha valley (the failed boat Gertie, sledges, snowshoe relays, caches), the climb out by way of the Goldie River and their mistaken reading of the Elwha's bend, the passage over Low Divide, the rain-forest descent of the North Fork Quinault, the raft wreck on the Quinault, and their arrival at Lake Quinault, the coast and Aberdeen in May 1890. Wood reconstructs the route day by day from the members' diaries and the Seattle Press report of 16 July 1890, ties their camps and blazes to today's trail, and explains the dozens of place names the party gave.

books.what_it_covers_own_words: Two books in one. Part one is a portrait of the peninsula: weather, rocks and landforms, plant zones from rain forest to alpine, wildlife, the human story from the coastal explorers onward, and the long political fight that produced Olympic National Park. Part two is a region-by-region trail guide, each chapter with its own map and an introduction to the terrain, plus logs of the beach routes along the coast, written with Wood's personal commentary rather than bare mileages. Library catalog blurbs stress that it doubles as an alarm about threats to the park's irreplaceable resources (North Olympic Library System record).

books.what_it_covers_own_words: The definitive study of Lt. Joseph P. O'Neil's two Army explorations: the 1885 reconnaissance south from Port Angeles over the first ranges toward the Dungeness and Mount Anderson country, cut short by transfer orders; and the 1890 Olympic Exploring Expedition, run jointly with the Oregon Alpine Club, which built a mule trail from Lake Cushman up the North Fork Skokomish, over the divides and down the East Fork Quinault, while foot parties fanned out across the southern half of the range and a side party claimed the first ascent of Mount Olympus. Wood follows the parties nearly day by day, using O'Neil's reports and the diaries of expedition members (above all Pvt. Harry Fisher), and includes material on the 1889-90 Press Expedition for context. He also traces O'Neil's recommendation that the interior become a national park. The catalog summary frames it the same way: 1885 was a partial reconnaissance of the northeastern Olympics; 1890 explored the southern half of the peninsula in depth (North Olympic Library System record).

books.what_it_covers_own_words: Trail-by-trail descriptions of the constructed trails and the 'way trails' (unmaintained or boot-beaten routes) of the Olympic Mountains, in both the national park and the surrounding national forest, grouped into parts by area. Entries describe the route, distances and elevations, junctions and camps, often with a note on history or natural features (general description from reviews and the publisher; not checked entry by entry). It became the standard guide to the Olympic backcountry (UW finding aid calls it the standard hiking guide to the park). Wood researched it on field trips from the 1950s into the mid-1980s; his trip notes are filed by year in his papers.

books.what_it_covers_own_words: A shorter, general-reader history of how the Olympic Mountains went from 'unknown' to national park: Native and settler-era legends about the interior, the maritime explorers, the burst of expeditions in 1889-90 (Press party, O'Neil, the Gilmans, Banta and Sharp, Wickersham's Banner party), the summer outings of climbing clubs to Mount Olympus in the early 1900s (The Mountaineers, the Explorers Club), and the campaign that led from Mount Olympus National Monument to Olympic National Park. Condensed by Wood from a 250-page manuscript to about 150 pages over ten years (1985-1995). The publisher's blurb promises previously unpublished historical photographs and detailed maps of the explorers' routes (North Olympic Library System record).

indigenous_history_guidance.principle: The Olympic Peninsula is the homeland of the Hoh, Quileute, Makah, Quinault, Klallam (Lower Elwha Klallam, Jamestown S'Klallam, Port Gamble S'Klallam), Skokomish and other peoples. Wood's books are settler-era exploration histories; they mention Native guides, packers, villages and legends from the explorers' point of view.
rules_for_this_file: Nothing here retells a Native story, and the game must not adapt the 'legend' material in The Land That Slept Late.

When a Wood fact involves Native people (the 1885 guide who left O'Neil's party; Native people who aided the lost Linsley-party man on the Queets; 'Indian packers' in 1890; the Imperial Eagle killings behind the name 'Destruction'), state it plainly, do not dramatize it, and flag it for review with the relevant nation before it appears in game text.
Many 'first' claims in Wood's narratives mean first recorded by settlers; the game should say 'first recorded' or 'first documented', not 'first ever'.

topical_index.title: The Seattle Press Exploring Expedition, Dec. 1889 - May 1890

facts.fact: The Seattle Press sponsored the party after Elisha P. Ferry, who was about to become the first governor of the State of Washington, publicly urged that someone explore the unknown interior of the Olympics; James H. Christie wrote offering to lead it.

Six men set out: James H. Christie (leader, a Scot with Canadian military and Arctic experience), Charles A. Barnes (topographer and photographer), John H. Crumback (cook), Christopher O. Hayes, John W. Sims, and Dr. Harries (or Harris) B. Runnalls, who quit on 3 Feb. 1890. Five finished.
They took four dogs, two mules and about 1,500 lb of supplies, left Seattle by steamer on 8 Dec. 1889, and set off from the end of the county road south of Port Angeles on 13 Dec.

Their flat-bottomed boat Gertie, built to haul gear up the Elwha, leaked and was given up after only a few miles of hard work; a sledge scheme also failed. They did not make real progress until mid-February, then moved up the valley on snowshoes, relaying loads between caches.

They reached the Lillian River area by 1 April. In April, after climbing up the Goldie River and nearby ridges, they realized they had mistaken a bend of the Elwha for the Quinault; they cached most of their gear and pushed on.

In early May they crossed the low saddle between the Elwha and the Quinault, which they called Elwha Pass (now Low Divide, about 3,650 ft). Coming up between Mount Seattle and Mount Christie they named Lake Mary and then Lake Margaret, at first thinking the ground between the lakes was the divide; the true divide lay just beyond. Barnes climbed Mount Seattle, and the party killed three bears, a welcome change from weeks of flour soup.

Going down the North Fork Quinault, a raft wreck cost them their guns and most specimens; Barnes got one pack out of the water, and it held the journals, the photographic negatives and the map. With help from a hunting party and a settler's canoe they reached Lake Quinault on 19 May and the ocean on 20 May 1890, and were photographed in Aberdeen on 21 May.
Animals: the dogs were Daisy, Bud, Tweed and Dike (Dike was killed by an elk); the mule Jennie died in a fall and Dollie was turned loose. No man died; the animals were the only losses.

The full report filled the Seattle Press of 16 July 1890 and gave the first broadly accurate picture of the range's layout; many of the party's names are still on the map, and their blazes can still be found along the Elwha trail.
Wood judged the Press crossing the first organized crossing of the range but credited O'Neil's 1890 expedition with the more thorough examination of the country.

topical_index.node_mapping_notes: Exact camp sites are in ATOM; the node list is the modern trail corridor the party roughly followed (the party detoured up the Goldie River, which has no node). Seattle Times 1997 places their start near today's Whiskey Bend trailhead.

topical_index.title: Names the Press party put on the map

facts.fact: At least eighteen Press names are still in use. Many peaks honor newspapermen and patrons: the Bailey Range (William E. Bailey, Press publisher), Mount Meany (Edmond S. Meany of the Press), Mount Dana (Charles Dana, New York Sun), Mount Noyes (Crosby Noyes, Washington Evening Star), Mount Scott (James W. Scott, Chicago Herald), Mount Ferry (the governor), Mount Seattle, plus Mount Christie and Mount Barnes for the explorers.

Some Press names did not stick or were never made official: Mount Pulitzer (for Joseph Pulitzer; also called Snagtooth), Mount Childs (for George W. Childs of the Philadelphia Ledger), and Mount Hearst (now Mount Queets).

Lakes and rivers were often named for women: Lake Mary and Lake Margaret at Low Divide, and the Lillian River. Semple Plateau honors territorial governor Eugene Semple; Press Valley (the upper Elwha) honors the paper itself; the Hayes River is named for party member Christopher Hayes.
Goblins Gate (Goblin Gates), the narrow Elwha gorge, got its name from Barnes, who in March 1890 saw a crowd of grim faces in the rock walls.

Geyser Valley was NOT a Press name: it is credited to an early-1900s resident nicknamed 'Doc' Ludden, who likened wind-whipped cloud columns to geysers. (Wood's ATOM index includes 'Geyser Valley', but only as a place the party passed.)

topical_index.node_mapping_notes: ferry_basin lies under Mount Ferry; lone_tree_pass is also called Pulitzer Pass; scott_ludden_saddle touches Mount Scott; bear_pass is near Mount Childs; queets_basin is under Mount Queets (Press 'Mount Hearst'). Lake Lillian (Grand Valley) is a different feature from the Lillian River; check the name origin before crediting the Press.

topical_index.title: Lt. Joseph P. O'Neil's first expedition, July-August 1885

facts.fact: The Army had already tried the Olympics: in 1882 Lts. Willis Wittich and Thomas H. Bradley cut a trail from Fort Townsend across both forks of the Dungeness, and in 1884 Lts. Charles M. Truitt and Willson Y. Stamper spent ten days trying to reopen it.

O'Neil, 14th Infantry, served at Fort Townsend July 1884 - April 1885, heard little reliable about the interior, and after moving to Vancouver Barracks talked Gen. Nelson A. Miles into an exploration, authorized 6 July 1885.

The party left Port Angeles on 17 July 1885 heading south; their Native guide slipped away the first night at the foot of the mountains. Blocked by forest and cliffs on the Elwha line, O'Neil turned toward Mount Angeles, meaning to follow the high divide southeast to the Dungeness headwaters and then the range's center.

Work days ran from about six in the morning to six at night on thin rations (bacon and salt pork, beans, flour, coffee) because hunting went badly; the mules kept slipping and tumbling down the steep sidehills. By 24 July they were at the foot of the first snowy range, and in under a month they had crossed it and made their base camp on the next ridge inland, where an abandoned hunters' cabin showed others had been there before.

From the Mount Angeles - Klahhane Ridge heights ('The Sisters') O'Neil took a cluster of peaks to the south for Mount Olympus. The party moved on to Hurricane Ridge and split: engineer Harry Hawgood's group headed for the Elwha but lost its supplies in a river crossing and turned back; O'Neil's group went southeast along the divide.

O'Neil left the mules at a camp he called 'Noplace' (probably Cameron Basin) and went on foot with Pvt. John Johnson toward the Mount Anderson country; the two became separated, and Johnson walked out alone. A courier then ordered O'Neil to Fort Leavenworth, ending the trip; he sailed from Port Angeles on 26 Aug.
Mount Claywood carries the name of Asst. Adjutant General H. Clay Wood, who signed the 1885 orders.

topical_index.node_mapping_notes: The 1885 route is reconstructed, not exact. 'Noplace' = probably Cameron Basin (Evans). Mount Claywood rises near the Cameron/Dosewallips headwaters.

topical_index.title: The Olympic Exploring Expedition (O'Neil and the Oregon Alpine Club), July-Oct. 1890

facts.fact: O'Neil, back in the Northwest from Aug. 1887 and secretary of the Oregon Alpine Club (founded 23 Sept. 1887), got a joint expedition approved: the club supplied three scientists and most of the money; the Army (Gen. John Gibbon) supplied O'Neil, ten enlisted men, a civilian packer, about a dozen mules and several dogs.

The scientists were Louis F. Henderson (botanist), Nelson E. Linsley (mining engineer and geologist) and Bernard J. Bretherton (naturalist). Enlisted and civilian members included Cpl. Frederick Haffner and Pvts. John Danton, John Bairens, Harry Fisher (the diarist Wood relied on), Higgins, Hughes, Kranichfeld and Krause, with civilians Frederic Church and M. Price.

The goal was to cross the range east to west in about three months, explore some 1,600 square miles, build a mule trail, and leave a copper box with a register on the summit of Mount Olympus. Supplies for about 100 days weighed roughly four tons, so the pack train had to relay.

The men gathered at Fort/Port Townsend on 26 June; on 1 July a steamer landed them at Lilliwaup on Hood Canal (not Hoodsport as planned). They bogged down in a swamp on the trail to Lake Cushman, rafted across the lake, and made Camp 1 on the west shore near settlers' farms.

A miners' trail ran about five miles up the North Fork Skokomish to a copper camp, the last outpost; just beyond, a cliff at the river's edge (named Fisher's Bluff after one of the men) forced them to cut a way up and over it; Camp 2 was nearby. The cedar 'staircase' the expedition built over a bluff here is the source of the name Staircase.
facts.confidence: medium-high (Wood names Fisher's Bluff; NPS audio tour ties the Staircase name to the expedition; that the two bluffs are the same is our inference)

facts.fact: Work days ran from six in the morning to seven at night, and the river was full of trout, so the men still went fishing after supper.

Near Camp 5 a box canyon stopped the mules until the men bridged it; they called it Jumbo's Leap for the old dog Jumbo, who went into it sooner than stay behind. By the end of July the trail was only about twelve miles long, and the crew was still deep in the canyon.

On 17 Aug. three foot parties went out: one explored the Duckabush and Dosewallips to Hood Canal, one went south over the southern rivers, and O'Neil's own party looked over the Quinault and Humptulips country on the way to Grays Harbor, while the rest pushed the mule trail to a base camp on the main divide.

A scouting party found a pass the mules could use, later named O'Neil Pass; the men set up Camp 15 on the Quinault side and finished the trail from the pass down to the Quinault. For the last foot trips each man carried about 60 lb.

The Linsley party left Camp 15 on 13 Sept., worked northwest to the base of Mount Olympus, and on 22 Sept. Linsley, Bretherton and Danton reached a summit on the south side; Wood thought their summit was most likely one of the rocky points of the South Peak, not the true top. The copper box has never been found. One man got separated and walked down the Queets alone to the ocean, where Native people helped him.

Short of shoes and food, the Linsley party skipped its assigned Hoh and Quillayute exploration and followed the Queets to the coast. The mules got to the Quinault forks on 24 Sept.; the explorers were feted at Hoquiam on 4 Oct. and disbanded on 6 Oct.; the Oregon Alpine Club gave them a banquet in Portland on 22 Oct.
Places named for the expedition include Mount Anderson (Col. Thomas M. Anderson), Mounts Bretherton, Church, Henderson, O'Neil and Steel (William G. Steel), O'Neil Pass, O'Neil Peak and O'Neil Creek.
Other parties met the expedition in the mountains: Wickersham's Banner party at the camp on Five Stream, and the Higley family at Hart Lake near O'Neil Pass.

topical_index.node_mapping_notes: The expedition's mule trail is the ancestor of today's North Fork Skokomish - First Divide - Duckabush - O'Neil Pass - East Fork Quinault route (Evans: sections of O'Neil trail are in today's system). Lake Cushman, Lilliwaup, Five Stream, Jumbo's Leap and Camp Nellie Bly have no nodes. queets_basin and the Queets nodes are Linsley-party ground.

topical_index.title: From 'terra incognita' to Olympic National Park

facts.fact: In his report submitted 16 Nov. 1890 O'Neil judged the interior of little practical value and recommended making it a national park, partly to protect the elk; he repeated the idea in a Portland lecture on 6 Dec. 1890.
James Wickersham, after his 1890 trip, drew what is thought to be the first map outlining a national park in the Olympics.

President Theodore Roosevelt proclaimed Mount Olympus National Monument on 2 March 1909; the Park Service took it over in 1933; Congress created Olympic National Park on 29 June 1938, about four weeks before the death of O'Neil, who had risen to brigadier general.

Preston P. Macy, custodian of the monument from 1934, became the park's first superintendent (1938-1951) and ran it at first from the attic of his Port Angeles home; Wood wrote a short biography of him.
facts.confidence: high (Macy facts from Macy finding aid)

topical_index.node_mapping_notes: Park-wide topic; port_angeles_wic is the natural place for it (park HQ town). The elk link is thematic.

topical_index.title: The crowded years: Gilman, Banta and Sharp, Wickersham, Higley, prospectors

facts.fact: Charles A. Gilman (former lieutenant governor of Minnesota) and his son Samuel traced the Quinault from the ocean toward its headwaters in late 1889 and reported widely on the country's resources (National Geographic, 1896).

J. J. Banta and S. P. Sharp traveled from Tacoma around the Strait of Juan de Fuca to Pysht Bay and then south through the country to Grays Harbor, 3 Dec. 1889 - Jan. 1890; Wood studied Banta's diary.

In 1890 Judge James Wickersham led the Buckley Banner party (men and women, several family members) up the North Fork Skokomish, met O'Neil's men at Five Stream, meant to come out by the Elwha but instead descended the Dosewallips to Hood Canal, about 125 miles on foot, back in Tacoma 10 Aug. He had also gone some 20 miles up the Skokomish in 1889.

Alfred Higley and his son Orte crossed from Hoodsport over the Duckabush divide to Hart Lake, met the O'Neil party, camped at Little O'Neil Creek, and came down the East Fork Quinault to settle at Lake Quinault in Oct. 1890.
In Aug. 1890 prospectors Pratt and Thompson, crossing south to north, found several Press camps on the North Fork Quinault and Elwha and climbed (probably) Mount Christie, calling it Kelley's Peak.

topical_index.node_mapping_notes: Wickersham's exact pass between the Skokomish and the Dosewallips is not given in our sources; do not draw it on the map yet.

facts.fact: Melbourne Watkinson's five-man party left Lilliwaup on Hood Canal on 2 Sept. 1878 and went west to Lake Cushman; in Wood's view it was a private trip that barely got into the mountains, not a true crossing.

topical_index.title: Sailors' names on the peninsula

facts.fact: Wood's park history in Trail Country covers the maritime explorers: the Spanish 1603 claim of Martin Aguilar, Barkley's 1787 naming of the Hoh as 'Destruction River' after crewmen of the Imperial Eagle were killed ashore, the Spanish naming of Port of Our Lady of the Angels (Port Angeles), Francisco de Eliza's 1791 post at Discovery Bay, and how Meares's 1788 'Mount Olympus' came to name the whole range and peninsula.

wood.locator: ch. 1 'The Land That Slept Late', p. 9; note p. 161 on Heceta

topical_index.indigenous_caution: The 'Destruction' story is told from the ships' side. Any in-game use touching the Hoh River mouth must be reviewed with the Hoh Tribe and Quileute Nation.

topical_index.title: Who climbed Mount Olympus first, and how

facts.fact: 1890: the O'Neil expedition's Linsley party reached a south-side summit (probably a crag of the South Peak, per Wood).

1899: Jack McGlone of the USGS survey climbed the East Peak. 1907: an Explorers Club of New York party climbed the Middle Peak, and The Mountaineers of Seattle made the first ascent of the West (true) summit on their first summer outing.

wood.locator_basis: chapter title and index terms via google_books_toc; specific facts from HistoryLink 7473, which lists LTSL among its sources

facts.fact: 1908: four climbers from Bremerton reached the West, Middle and East peaks in a single day.
In his papers Wood noted that Humes Glacier was named by climbers of the New York Explorers Club, not by The Mountaineers as a 1970s placard at Humes Ranch said.

wood.locator: Carton V/misc. item (e): note on Humes Ranch placard

facts.fact: Wood himself climbed Olympus many times (eighteen ascents per his death notice, seen via search summary) and left an unpublished essay titled 'Mount Olympus, Least of the Six Majors' (contents not seen).

topical_index.node_mapping_notes: The modern Hoh route is not the 1907 approach; the early club parties came by other valleys (LTSL index lists Elwha Basin, Queets Basin, Soleduck River, Hoh River). Do not claim a specific 1907 route for a node until LTSL is checked.

topical_index.title: Humes Ranch and the middle Elwha

facts.fact: The Press party worked up this stretch of the Elwha in Feb.-March 1890 and named Goblins Gate.

Wood kept a history of Humes Ranch in his O'Neil research files and corrected the ranch placard's claim about who named Humes Glacier. (That Will Humes guided the 1907 Explorers Club party is general knowledge, not yet checked against Wood.)
The Press party named the range for William E. Bailey, publisher of the Seattle Press.

In August 1961 Bob Wood, Doug Waali and Kent Heathershaw made reported first ascents of Mount Childs (6,205 ft; Aug. 6, an easy scramble up east-side talus), Mount Pulitzer (6,283 ft; by a splintered east ridge) and Stephen Peak (6,430 ft; Aug. 8, from upper Cream Lake basin).
facts.confidence: medium-high (identity of 'Bob Wood' very probable, not proven)

facts.fact: Wood wrote an unpublished true account titled 'A Trip up the Bailey'; his trail guide covers the range's way trails (index term 'Bailey Range').

topical_index.title: Trails, camps and way trails (the trail-guide layer)

facts.fact: For any trail, junction, shelter site or way trail in the park or Olympic National Forest, Wood's Olympic Mountains Trail Guide (1984-2000; updated 2020 by Hoke, Savage and the Peninsula Wilderness Club) is the standard description; Trail Country (1968) and Wilderness Trails (1970) record the trail system and beach routes as they were around 1968-70, useful for 'how it used to be' notes (old shelters, abandoned trails).
Example locator: the 2nd edition (1991) begins Part I on p. 23, with the Barnes Creek Trail on p. 31.
The 3rd edition's catalog blurb highlights the Cat Creek Way Trail, a high route with a view of Oyster Lake, and the Appleton Pass Trail with its boulder-sitting marmots.

topical_index.node_mapping_notes: This topic applies to every trail node; only the nodes with a verified page are listed. Coast nodes: use TC/WT beach logs, not OMTG (coverage unverified).

topical_index.title: The wilderness coast in Wood's early guides

facts.fact: Trail Country (1968) and its spin-off Wilderness Trails of Olympic National Park (1970) include beach logs for the park's coastal strip alongside the mountain trail logs.

topical_index.node_mapping_notes: Which beaches the logs cover is not yet checked; nodes listed are the main beach-route anchors.

facts.fact: Wood's first serious writing on the Olympics was a 1948 University of Washington term paper on the Olympic rain forest, which he later called the seed of his books; Trail Country's natural-history half covers the rain-forest plant community.

Wood wrote a 117-page memorandum on Olympic place names (Dec. 1984 - Jan. 1985) and written remarks correcting Olympic entries in Robert Hitchman's 'Place Names of Washington' (1986). Both are at UW Special Collections and are the place to check before writing any 'named for...' line for a node.

topical_index.title: Staircase and the North Fork Skokomish

facts.fact: In 1890 Lake Cushman's west shore had settlers' farms (Windhoffer's clover-and-timothy field and a solid, well-furnished house; neighbors named Davis, McCabe, Muller, Stebbins and Church), copper claims were being worked above the lake, and a deserted hunter's lean-to stood near Five Stream.
Wood wrote 'Hiking the Skokomish' for the Peninsula Daily News and an unpublished piece on a Skokomish forest fire.

topical_index.title: The West End (Hoh and Queets country)

facts.fact: Wood's unpublished 1981 manuscript 'Beyond Olympus: The West End of Jefferson County', written from Bob Brown's materials, is the Wood-family source for settler history of the Hoh and Queets valleys; he also wrote a piece on Kloochman Rock in the Queets valley.
The Linsley party of 1890 came down the Queets after the Olympus climb.
